summary:
Gwangju stands under South Korea's national framework. Gender identity and gender expression are not criminalised in civilian life, and consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal. The exception is the armed forces: Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, the Constitutional Court upheld the provision in 2023, and a gay soldier received a six-month sentence in 2017. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

The principal trans-specific protection on the ground is a finalised court judgment on restroom access. On 22 July 2024 a Seoul appellate court dismissed the state's appeal and finalised a 300,000 won damages award against a claim of 3 million won, holding that police advice telling a person transitioning from male to female, whose family-register gender change had been approved by a court in 2020, to avoid women's public restrooms infringed personal rights. The court held that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right. The judgment is unappealed and binds as national framework for Gwangju.

The practical conditions behind that ruling are documented. A 2021 survey by the National Human Rights Commission of Korea of 591 transgender respondents found that 41% avoided facilities out of fear. Earlier relief exists at private level: a 2021 damages award against a private academy that barred a student from school restrooms.

Legal gender recognition is available and the surgical requirement has fallen. On 8 May 2024 a district court in Yeongdong approved changing the registered sex from male to female for five transgender applicants without sex-reassignment surgery, holding that conditioning gender change on surgery is against the law and that court guidelines requiring surgery now serve as reference rather than criteria. The court stated that every human being has the right to form their character and live a life according to their gender identity. The Supreme Court has separately allowed a transgender person with minor children to change gender in the family relations register.

No comprehensive anti-discrimination law covers sexual orientation or gender identity, so services, employment and accommodation in Gwangju carry no statutory protection on these grounds. In healthcare the National Human Rights Commission of Korea flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation in November 2023, after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, stating that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

There is no same-sex marriage, which affects a visitor travelling with a partner. The Constitutional Court did issue a 2024 ruling extending recognition of same-sex partners' healthcare rights in that specific area.

Organised conservative opposition is active nationally, Human Rights Watch records persistent discrimination against LGBT people in its 2025 world report, and there is no national anti-discrimination statute to counter it, although the same report notes a relatively positive overall record for free media and civil society. No severe incident involving a trans visitor is documented in these sources.
tangentialFactors:
The trajectory of the courts matters to how a visitor reads local friction. Two 2024 rulings cut in the same direction on distinct issues: one removed sex-reassignment surgery as a precondition for registered-sex change, the other treated police advice to avoid women's restrooms as an infringement of personal rights. Both are national in reach and neither is confined to the capital.

Facility avoidance is measured rather than assumed. The 2021 National Human Rights Commission survey of 591 transgender respondents recorded 41% staying away from facilities out of fear, which indicates the gap between the formal right recognised by the courts and daily practice.

Private institutions have been held liable. The 2021 damages award against a private academy shows that exclusion by non-state actors has produced a monetary judgment, even though no general anti-discrimination statute exists to underwrite such claims.

Compared with the security environment in many jurisdictions, the residual risk in Gwangju sits in social opposition and the absence of statutory protection rather than in criminal law. Human Rights Watch pairs its findings of persistent discrimination with a relatively positive overall record for free media and civil society.
localsOnly:
Residents may change registered sex without undergoing surgery, following the 8 May 2024 ruling that court guidelines requiring surgery are reference material rather than criteria, and a transgender parent may change gender in the family relations register while retaining minor children.

Residents have a judicially settled right to use public restrooms corresponding to their gender, with the state liable in damages for advising otherwise. The 2021 award against a private academy extends that logic to private premises.

Employment, services and accommodation offer no statutory protection against discrimination on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation, and the Ministry of Health and Welfare has declined to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients.

Transgender residents are excluded from military service, and service members remain exposed to prosecution under Military Criminal Act article 92-6, upheld by the Constitutional Court in 2023.

Same-sex couples cannot marry, though the Constitutional Court's 2024 ruling gives same-sex partners a defined measure of healthcare recognition.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Gwangju Metropolitan City or its police and medical institutions have issued any local ordinance, directive or guideline specific to transgender residents is not sourced in this inventory; only national rulings and national bodies are covered.

The jurisdiction, court and parties of the 2021 private-academy restroom damages award are not specified in the sources provided, so its territorial applicability beyond the national framework is unresolved.

The identity of the appellate court that finalised the 300,000 won award on 22 July 2024, and whether any further extraordinary remedy was sought after that date, are not stated.

No source in the inventory records any incident involving a transgender visitor in Gwangju; the absence of such a record should not be read as a finding of safety.

Whether the May 2024 ruling without surgery has been applied uniformly by the courts handling Gwangju residents, and how many applications it has produced, is not sourced.
